Or, why the psychophysical law is a stretched exponential function

This page was assembled by an AI agent from the outputs of the registered analysis scripts in ign-ratings/scripts/ (see scripts/REGISTRY.md). Prose has not been line-by-line verified by a human; do not publish or cite as-is. All statistics are read directly from the scripts’ processed_data/ outputs, not recomputed here.

Overview

This page collects one set of analyses run identically across three very different rating systems:

  1. IGN video game ratings (integer 1–10, 2020–2025) against Steam outcome data — a purely subjective, evaluative categorization: game quality has no discernible objective correlate (no retinal neurons registering photons, not even an implicit tally of exposures — just an aesthetic/hedonic evaluation), yet that evaluation has real-world correlates we can measure, player counts and sales;
  2. historical stellar magnitudes (brightness classes 1–6, assigned by 14 observers from Ptolemy in 137 AD to Piazzi in 1814) against modern photometric flux — an objective perceptual categorization: a physical magnitude arriving at the eye, categorized by scientists as a measurement of that magnitude; and
  3. word familiarity norms (Glasgow Norms, 1–7 scale) against corpus word frequency — an experiential categorization of an objective quantity: how often you encounter a word is an objective count, but nothing perceives it directly — the judgment reads accumulated experience out of memory.

The test is in that sense fully general: the same battery runs on a perceptual categorization of a physical magnitude, a memory-based categorization of an objective exposure count, and a pure aesthetic evaluation with no objective correlate at all — three different kinds of judgment, three unrelated corners of the space of things a rating scale can do. Finding the same spacing law in all three would otherwise be what Meehl (1990), borrowing Wesley Salmon’s (1984) phrase, called a damn strange coincidence: theories earn credence by predicting facts that, absent the theory, would be antecedently improbable — and the agreement below is exactly that kind of fact.

One disambiguation, used strictly throughout: the IGN data come from video game reviews, and the sales proxy is the count of Steam user reviews — two different things that share a word. On this page, rating always refers to the IGN 1–10 score, and reviews always refers to the Steam review count (the sales proxy).

The same basic pattern appears in all three. Throughout, the objective quantity paired with each rating — review counts, player counts, photometric flux, corpus frequency — is called the stimulus: the magnitude the score is treated as categorizing. When an ordinal rating scale is treated as a categorization of the stimulus measured in log-stimulus space, the category boundaries are not equally spaced. Instead each successive category is wider than the one below it by a roughly constant multiplicative factor — a geometric progression of category widths, with ratio r ≈ 1.24–1.27 for IGN ratings, r ≈ 1.17 for stellar magnitudes (1.16 with a pre/post-telescope era control; Section 6.6), and r ≈ 1.41 for word familiarity. Note what is and isn’t constant: the raw stimulus ratio per step is not constant (that would be a logarithmic scale) — it is the step size in log-stimulus coordinates that grows by the constant ratio r, so the raw per-step stimulus ratios themselves compound.

An equivalent description on the category means:

\[\log \Phi = c + A\,e^{\beta S},\]

where Φ is the stimulus (reviews, players, flux, corpus frequency), S is the rating, c is an additive floor (the log-stimulus level the scale bottoms out at), A is a scale constant, and β is the growth rate — the log of the width ratio r, so β = ln r. In terms of the rating this says log-stimulus compounds: each rating step multiplies (log Φ − c) by e^β = r. Under the reading S = k·log ψ (ψ the latent magnitude) the same equation becomes log Φ = c + A′·ψ^(βk) with βk < 1 — the stretched exponential in ψ from which this page takes its name. One line to keep the fitted and the inferred separate: what is literally fit to data, everywhere on this page, is the S-space form — fixed log-stimulus ratios — and the analyses test the SE law through that observable signature; the final step from the S-form to a stretched exponential in ψ is inferred through S = k·log ψ, not fit. In every dataset the fixed-log-stimulus-ratio mean function beats the fixed-stimulus- ratio (Fechnerian) alternative, and a power law in the raw stimulus loses badly. Section 2 derives the form from first principles, introduces the function properly, and says where it sits in the history of psychophysics.

Read headline numbers from processed_data 
library(dplyr); library(jsonlite); library(knitr); library(ggplot2); library(tidyr)
pd <- "../processed_data"
r16 <- read_json(file.path(pd, "16_results.json"))
r73 <- read_json(file.path(pd, "73_results.json"))
r71 <- read_json(file.path(pd, "71_results.json"))
n58 <- read.csv(file.path(pd, "58_norms.csv"))[1, ]

tibble::tribble(
  ~Dataset, ~Rating, ~`Stimulus (log)`, ~n, ~`Geometric ratio r`,
  "IGN × peak concurrent players", "IGN 5–10 (integer era)", "log all-time peak concurrent players",
    r73$n, round(r73$geometric_r, 3),
  "IGN × Steam reviews", "IGN 5–10", "log Steam total reviews",
    r16$steam$n, round(r16$steam$geom_r, 3),
  "IGN console-inclusive", "IGN 5–10", "log Metacritic user-rating count",
    r16$full$n, round(r16$full$geom_r, 3),
  "Stellar magnitudes", "brightness class 1–6", "log relative flux (Hipparcos V)",
    r71$preera$battery$n, round(r71$preera$battery$thresholds$pooled$geom$r, 3),
  "Word familiarity", "Glasgow FAM 1–7 (rounded item means)", "SUBTLEX-UK Zipf frequency",
    n58$n, round(n58$r_geom, 3)
) |> kable()

Here r is the estimated common ratio of successive category widths, read from the threshold spacing of a graded response model anchored to log stimulus (the GRM — the standard psychometric model for ordered categories; Section 5 is the supplement that explains it); r = 1 would mean equally spaced categories in log stimulus (“Fechnerian” spacing — fixed stimulus ratios per category), r > 1 means categories widen going up the scale (fixed log-stimulus ratios, per the title).

The stellar sample is restricted to the pre-telescope sky — telescopic-era observers enter only on stars a pre-telescopic catalog contains (Section 6); a pre/post-telescope era control barely moves its r (Section 6.6).

Reproducibility. Every number on this page is read from processed_data/ files written by the numbered, registered scripts in scripts/ (index: scripts/REGISTRY.md; seed 42 throughout). The page performs no new analysis: it loads result JSONs and CSVs and displays them. Figures are the scripts’ own PNG outputs (script number in each caption) or simple plots of per-category summary tables.

Where the stretched exponential comes from

Two dueling psychophysical laws

In the history of psychophysics there are two dueling candidates for the psychophysical law — the function governing the relationship between the physical world (a physical stimulus like the objective number of photons hitting your eye — the Φ of the equation above) and the mind (a psychological magnitude like the intensity of a perceptual experience — in this example subjective brightness; the ψ).

Fechner (1860) proposed a logarithmic law, ψ = log Φ: each ratio change of the stimulus (say, a doubling) produces a constant additive change in psychological magnitude. He proposed measuring psychological magnitude by summing units of just-noticeable differences (JNDs) in the stimulus — because the JND captures stimulus ratios. Consider the difference between a 2-inch line and a 3-inch line: to reproduce that same subjective difference at a larger size, you need to put a 30-inch line next to the 20-inch one (50% bigger), not a 21-inch line (1 inch longer). Stimuli must differ by a constant ratio to be equally discriminable — the constant is the Weber fraction, and the general principle is Weber’s law. (There is a good case that Weber’s law is a property of physics, not perception — measurement error in general behaves this way, and for naturally fluctuating intensities constant relative error is what an optimal receiver of any kind achieves: Pednekar, Krishnadas, Cho & Makris 2023, Proc. R. Soc. A 479:20220626.)

Modern psychometrics implicitly inherits Fechner’s identification. Thurstone (1927) was explicit about it: his law of comparative judgment builds the psychological scale out of confusability, with the discriminal dispersion — the standard deviation of the momentary judgment process — as the unit of the continuum, so that equal scale distances just are equal discriminability. Luce and Edwards (1958) showed how that summation must be done to be internally consistent — and that it yields a logarithmic scale only if Weber’s law holds exactly — while insisting that equal JNDs are a convention, not a discovery about felt magnitude. And the same move defines the modern latent-trait scales: a Rasch or IRT θ is measured in units of response noise (a logit or probit step is one standard-deviation-of-judgment’s worth of endorsement probability), as is signal detection’s d′ (distance in noise-SD units). Any scale whose unit is variance — wherever noise is what gets summed to produce the psychological continuum — is a JND-count scale, and so silently assumes Fechner’s identification of experience with discrimination units, rather than asking, with Stevens, how felt magnitude grows across those units.

Stevens (1957) proposed a power law instead: ψ = Φ^a, the subjective intensity is the stimulus raised to a power. The exponent a is usually read off a log-log plot, where log ψ = a·log Φ is a straight line with slope a. A power law means equal ratio changes of the stimulus produce equal ratio changes of the psychological magnitude. That is perceptually useful, because ratios out in the world are what matter: if one stick is twice as long as another, it appears twice as long whether it is right in front of you or twenty yards away.

Stevens’ law collected its own embarrassments, though. Measured exponents refuse to behave like constants of nature: they drift with stimulus range, context, and procedure (Poulton 1968; Teghtsoonian 1973), and Shepard (1981) argued that direct scaling cannot, by itself, uniquely pin down the psychophysical function at all: a magnitude estimate is the composition of two mappings — stimulus into sensation, and sensation into the emitted number — and the judgments constrain only the composition, so any candidate ψ can be traded away against a compensating response function. And the law’s core virtue overreaches: strict scale invariance says perception preserves ratios and nothing else — no trace of absolute scale — when in fact we live in, and perceive, a world that is only approximately scale invariant. Hold both embarrassments; the stretched exponential answers them below.

What rating scales do: the psychometric law

Alongside the psychophysical law (world → mind, Φ → ψ), it is useful to name a second mapping: call the function from mind to measurement — from ψ to the reported score S — the psychometric law (my term; it is not an established one). My empirical work finds that this psychometric law is a logarithmic function of ψ — S = k·log ψ + const, with k the scale’s slope (Chituc & Santos, under review). Across pain, crime severity, and eight further subjective experiences (happiness, morality, beauty, desires, opinions, love, fear), subjects rated self-generated exemplars on both a standard 10-point self-report scale and a magnitude estimation scale: the self-report ratings are a near-perfect logarithmic compression of the magnitude estimates (median R² = .99), with each scale step worth a median ratio of ×1.9 (IQR [1.8, 2.0]) of underlying magnitude. Rating scales, in other words, work like decibels or earthquake magnitudes — they capture equal ratios of the thing they measure, and one scale point does roughly what 10 decibels does for perceived loudness (about a doubling — of the subjective magnitude, not the physical energy). The compression is drastic enough that the subjective midpoint of a 10-point scale sits near its top: the last point captures nearly as much subjective distance as the first nine combined. And the same work shows this is a fact about the report scale, not the judgments: magnitude estimates preserve additivity (sums of ratings track sums of experiences; completion-task slopes ≈ 1) and midpoint structure (bisection-task slopes ≈ 1), while self-report ratings are compressed on both.

This makes a rating scale something like the y-axis of Stevens’ log-log plot: if S is in effect log ψ, and Stevens is right that ψ = Φ^a, then S = a·log Φ + const. (One caveat: this route cannot recover a good estimate of a, because we do not know the base of the logarithm the psychological scale uses — a log-log slope is only exact when both axes use the same base; otherwise a is off by a multiplicative constant. None of that matters for anything here.) But note what that composition predicts: ratings linear in log stimulus — equal category widths in log-stimulus space. That is exactly the Fechnerian threshold model that loses in every dataset on this page.

A third law: a stretched exponential function

I have grown increasingly convinced that the psychophysical law is neither Fechner’s logarithm nor Stevens’ power law of the stimulus, but a third thing: Fechner was right that the fundamental unit is the JND, and Stevens was right about the functional form. Suppose perception follows a power law not of the stimulus per se but of the stimulus’s discriminability — the number of JNDs it sits above threshold, which by Weber’s law is a logarithmic function of the stimulus: n = log(Φ/Φ₀), with Φ₀ the threshold. Then

\[\psi = n^{\gamma} = \big(\log (\Phi/\Phi_0)\big)^{\gamma},\]

where n is the JND count, γ is the power-law exponent on it, and Φ₀ is the perceptual threshold.

One disambiguation before composing, because “JND” is doing partly metaphorical work here. A JND is a behavioral object — a discriminability judgment — and the claim is not that sensory transduction literally consumes discriminability judgments as inputs. The substantive claim is about the front end’s coordinates: a receiver that minimizes relative error has constant resolution in log-stimulus units, so its input arrives naturally denominated in resolvable steps — a quantity that counts stimulus ratios exactly as summed JNDs would. “JND count” is the convenient name for that coordinate because Fechner made it famous and because behavioral JNDs are how it was historically measured, but the law needs only the logarithmic input coordinate, not the psychophysics of discrimination itself. One consequence worth keeping in mind: the well-documented deviations in discrimination experiments — the near-misses to Weber’s law, for instance — are facts about discrimination judgments, and whether they propagate into this input coordinate is an open question, not an assumption of the account.

Compose this with the psychometric law S = k·log ψ + const and the rating becomes a log of the JND count:

\[S = k\gamma \cdot \log\big(\log (\Phi/\Phi_0)\big) + b,\]

with b collecting the constants. The world gets logged twice on its way to the scale — once by Weber (stimulus → discriminability units), once by the report scale (magnitude → category number). Solving for the stimulus given the rating — which is the direction the data on this page are fit in — gives

\[\log \Phi = c + A\,e^{\beta S}, \qquad c = \log \Phi_0, \quad \beta = \tfrac{1}{k\gamma},\]

exactly the mean function fitted throughout this page. Because the scale is a log of a log of the stimulus, going back from scale to world simply undoes the two logarithms — that is all the equation is. It packs several moves into one line, so here is the same equation read piece by piece, from the rating out to the stimulus:

  • Start with the rating S and scale it by β. Because β = 1/(kγ), this one constant undoes both stages of the mind’s compression at once: k (how many scale points the report scale assigns per ratio step of ψ) and γ (the power law relating ψ to the JND count). A small β means a lot of compression happened on the way in.
  • Exponentiate: e^(βS). This undoes the outer logarithm — the report scale’s. The result, scaled by A, is the JND count: n = A·e^(βS), the number of just-noticeable steps the stimulus sits above threshold. Note what the exponential does per rating point: each +1 in S multiplies the JND count by e^β — a constant factor. This is exactly where the geometric widths come from, r = e^β.
  • A is the anchor: at S = 0 the formula gives n = A, so A is the JND count where the scale’s zero sits — how far up the discriminability ladder the bottom of the scale is.
  • Add c = log Φ₀. The JND count is a count of ratio steps of stimulus (Weber), so it lives in log-stimulus units; to turn it into an absolute log-stimulus position you add the threshold, the stimulus level at zero JNDs. Below Φ₀ nothing is detectable, which is why the floor is not optional.
  • Read off log Φ = c + A·e^(βS): log stimulus = threshold + JND count. The whole law in one sentence: the rating indexes the JND count geometrically, and the JND count sits on top of the threshold in log-stimulus space.

This double-log structure is also exactly where the fixed log-stimulus ratios come from. A unit step of the rating adds a constant (β) two logs up — on log(log Φ − c). Adding a constant to a logarithm means multiplying the quantity underneath it: so one log up, the floored log-stimulus (log Φ − c) is multiplied by e^β = r with every step — the geometric category widths. And multiplying a logarithm means raising to a power underneath it: at ground level, each step raises the stimulus span above threshold to the power r. One constant, read at three depths of the ladder — additive at the top, multiplicative in the middle, a power at the bottom.

Substituting S = k·log ψ back in gives log Φ = c + A′·ψ^(βk) with βk < 1 — log-stimulus as a decelerating power law of the latent magnitude, every parameter now carrying a psychophysical meaning.

And to put this back in the original psychological frame, with the report scale gone entirely: the substitution turns e^(βS) into ψ^(βk) (the exponential of a logarithm is a power), so the rating S drops out and what remains is a relation between world and mind alone —

\[\Phi = \Phi_0 \, e^{A'\,\psi^{1/\gamma}},\]

or, in log form (removing the double exponent),

\[\log(\Phi/\Phi_0) = A'\,\psi^{1/\gamma}:\]

the world is a stretched exponential of the mind. This is the function the page is named for, so it deserves a proper introduction. A stretched exponential is an exponential whose argument has been compressed by a power less than one — y = e(A·xb) with 0 < b < 1; here x = ψ and b = 1/γ. At b = 1 it is an ordinary exponential; with b < 1 the growth is “stretched” over a much wider range, with no single characteristic scale. One logarithm removes the exponential and leaves a pure power law (that is the second display above); a second log straightens it into a line with slope b. The name comes from physics: the decaying version, f(t) = e(−(t/τ)b), is Kohlrausch’s (1854) relaxation law for disordered materials, and the family has had a modern revival as the disciplined alternative to power laws for heavy-tailed phenomena. Laherrère and Sornette (1998) showed that with just two interpretable parameters it describes the luminosities of galaxies, oilfield reserve sizes, urban agglomerations, country populations, daily currency fluctuations, the 400,000-year Vostok temperature record, the fossil extinction kill curve, earthquake sizes, and citation counts — and that it arises generically wherever a quantity is the product of finitely many random factors, the exponent b tracking the length of the multiplicative chain. Figure 2 shows the family in the increasing form used on this page.

This is also where Stevens’ two embarrassments dissolve. Under the stretched-exponential law the local Stevens exponent is not a constant: it is γ divided by the number of e-folds the stimulus sits above threshold (d log ψ / d log Φ = γ / log(Φ/Φ₀)) — so measured exponents should drift with range and level, exactly as Poulton and Teghtsoonian found. Yet the law still delivers what made the power law attractive, over the range where it matters: for a stimulus sitting n e-folds above threshold, the exponent is nearly constant across any span of δ e-folds with drift only of order δ/n. Far above threshold — where ecologically typical stimuli live, many e-folds up — ratio structure is preserved locally: the stick that is twice as long still looks twice as long. Near threshold, and across very wide ranges, the exponent bends lawfully — and that slow bend is not a bug but the signature of characteristic scale, the absolute-position information a strict power law would erase. A power law is tuned to a perfectly scale-invariant world; the stretched exponential is tuned to ours, which is only approximately so.

Shepard’s indeterminacy, meanwhile, is answered by how these analyses are built rather than by the law itself. Nothing on this page treats the reported number as a readout of ψ: the rating enters only as an ordinal category, and every empirical claim lives on the stimulus side — where the boundaries sit in log-stimulus space — a structure untouched by any monotone relabeling of the response scale, which is exactly the degree of freedom Shepard showed direct scaling cannot fix. The decomposition into psychophysical and psychometric halves is then constrained by independent evidence for the psychometric half (report scales log the mind), not by the scaling data being decomposed — and the one degree of freedom that genuinely remains, the log base k, is flagged as unidentified throughout rather than silently fixed.

Two remarks about the form as it appears here. Naming: the fitted S-form, log Φ = c + A·e^(βS), is an ordinary exponential in the rating; the relation is a stretched exponential specifically in ψ, because S = k·log ψ turns e^(βS) into the compressed power ψ^(βk) — an exponential of a logged variable just is a power law of the underlying one. Calling the mean function “stretched-exponential” throughout this page is shorthand licensed by that psychometric reading. Direction: read the other way, the same curve is the power-of-log law, ψ ∝ (log Φ/Φ₀)^γ — and nothing psychological hangs on which direction wears the logarithm. Inverting swaps the two forms (a stretched exponential undone is a power of a log), and the log of Φ is just the world re-expressed in its natural ratio coordinates — by Weber’s law only stimulus ratios carry information, so Φ’s unit, and with it the log’s base, is pure convention. One curve, two readings. So the psychophysical law that reconciles Fechner and Stevens — and with them reintegrates psychophysical scaling and the psychometric tradition that pulled apart from it about a century ago — can fairly be called a stretched exponential law. Note only that this reverses the classic direction in which the law is framed: psychophysics traditionally writes the law running from the world to the mind (ψ = f(Φ)), whereas the stretched-exponential form runs from the mind to the world (Φ = f(ψ)).

Equal unit changes of the rating should therefore produce equal ratio steps of the (floored) log stimulus — geometric category widths, with r = e^β. And the two rivals fall out of the same algebra as the two ways to break the chain: keep Fechner all the way (γ = 1) and log Φ is linear in S — flat step ratios; keep Stevens on the raw stimulus (skip the Weber log) and the step ratios decelerate. Only the double-log chain produces the accelerating ratios the data show (×1.32 → ×3.33 on peak players; ×1.35 → ×4.07 on reviews). That is what video game ratings, stellar magnitudes, and word familiarity all do — which presents a parsimonious reconciliation: the unit (the JND) goes to Fechner, and the form (the power law) goes to Stevens. Stated as errors: Fechner’s mistake was not where he put the logarithm but that he had only one log and asserted γ = 1 — identifying experience with the JND count itself, each detection step one equal unit of feeling (an identification the psychometric tradition inherited). Stevens’ mistake is the mirror image: right functional form, wrong argument. The mind does not take the raw stimulus as its input — no percept has access to photons-per-second as such. It takes the detected stimulus: what survives the sensory front end. And if that front end is an optimal receiver minimizing relative error — which is what Weber’s law amounts to, for the eye as for any well-designed instrument (Pednekar et al. 2023) — then the input to the psychophysical law arrives already denominated in discriminability: JND counts, in which equal steps are equal increments of resolvable evidence. Stevens applied his ratio-preserving power law to the physicist’s Φ, when the quantity actually crossing the receiver’s front door was log(Φ/Φ₀). Let his own law preserve ratios of the evidence rather than ratios of the energy, and it lands exactly on the third law above. Each was right about one half; the law above is both halves assembled.

The IGN dataset

Provenance

I met Tom Marks — Associate Reviews Director at IGN, so maybe not the guy who runs the reviews, but at least one of the guys — playing Magic: The Gathering at my local game store. I got very interested in how thoughtful they are about assigning ratings to games. That is my bread and butter. So I started digging.

IGN switched to whole-number 1–10 ratings in January 2020 (“integer era”). Ratings here come from the published Kaggle scrape davutb/metacritic-games (Metacritic snapshot 2025-03-16) — not scraped from IGN directly (Ziff Davis robots.txt prohibits automated harvesting). Coverage is partial: roughly 165 IGN ratings per year captured vs the 250+ IGN publishes.

Two stimulus measures are carried through the IGN analyses. The primary measure is play behavior; the review count is the secondary, corroborating measure:

  • All-time peak concurrent players (primary; script 06_fetch_more_outcomes.py): the highest number of players ever simultaneously in the game, scraped per-game from SteamCharts — a third-party archive that logs Valve’s official concurrent-player telemetry — in the fetch of 2026-08-12 (coverage: 525 of the 607 matched games; n = 508 in the ratings-5–10 analyses). No review-writing enters this pipeline at any point.
  • Steam total review count (secondary; script 03_fetch_steam_outcomes.py): from the official Steam appreviews API — a census-complete, official count of all user reviews ever posted for the game. It serves as a sales proxy (unit sales are roughly 20–90× the review count per title, the “Boxleiter” multiplier; this is a proxy, not unit sales).

In the psychophysical framing used throughout this page, these measures play the role of the stimulus — the objective magnitude the rating is treated as categorizing. One caveat, and how it resolves: unlike flux hitting an astronomer’s eye, raters never perceive player counts or future sales. But they are perceiving game quality. If concurrent players and sales are a proxy for game quality — a decently plausible assumption; I wouldn’t lose sleep if it didn’t work, but the results below are hard to explain otherwise if it does, and it does — then the logic carries through unchanged, with the two independent proxies serving as checks on each other.

Exclusion funnel

Code 
funnel <- read_json(file.path(pd, "01_funnel.json"))
read.csv(file.path(pd, "05_exclusion_funnel.csv")) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Step", "n"))

From 13312 raw IGN critic rows, 851 unique integer-era ratings of 841 games survive (published 2020-02-03 to 2025-03-12). Unmatched games are mostly console/Epic/VR exclusives and DLC.

Rating distribution, and why ratings 5 and up

Code 
sd <- funnel$score_distribution_1to10
ign_labels <- c(`1` = "Unbearable", `2` = "Painful", `3` = "Awful", `4` = "Bad",
                `5` = "Mediocre", `6` = "Okay", `7` = "Good", `8` = "Great",
                `9` = "Amazing", `10` = "Masterpiece")
dist <- tibble::tibble(score = as.integer(names(sd)), n = unlist(sd)) |>
  mutate(lab = ign_labels[as.character(score)], inside = n >= 100)
ggplot(dist, aes(n, factor(score, levels = 1:10))) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey30", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(x = ifelse(inside, n - 4, n + 4), label = lab,
                hjust = ifelse(inside, 1, 0), color = inside), size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "white", `FALSE` = "black"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Ratings", y = "IGN rating") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 11)

Each number on the scale is a named verbal category — IGN publishes a label for every integer, from 1 (“Unbearable”) up through 5 (“Mediocre”), 7 (“Good”), and 10 (“Masterpiece”) — so the 1–10 rating is an ordered set of named categories, not a bare number line. The mode is 8 (“Great”); 73% of ratings are 7–9; no game received a 1, and ratings 2–4 are sparse (n = 7, 5, 25).

The analyses on this page use ratings 5 (“Mediocre”) through 10 (“Masterpiece”) only. Beyond the sparsity, the 1–10 scale is bipolar: the labels run from bad through neutral to good — the bottom half is explicitly negative (4 “Bad”, 3 “Awful”, 2 “Painful”, 1 “Unbearable”) — and we don’t want to mix constructs. The neutral-to-good half tracks how good a game is; the full bad-to-neutral-to-good range would also be tracking how bad it is — a different construct. Restricting to “Mediocre”-and-up keeps the analysis on a single (unipolar) construct. The 5–10 samples are: n = 508 games on the primary measure (peak concurrent players), N = 560 Steam-matched games on the review-count measure, and N = 803 in the console-inclusive replication (all platforms, Metacritic user-rating count as the stimulus measure).

Standing caveats

  • Proxy stimulus measures. Peak concurrent players (the primary measure) confounds popularity with longevity, and Steam reviews are not unit sales (an independent calibration against developer-reported sales — script 18, GameDiscoverCo Oct-2022 survey, 199 games — gives log-units ~ log-reviews slope b = 1.087, R² = 0.925: reviews slightly understate the spread in sales).
  • Steam selection. 234 console/Epic/VR-exclusive games are excluded from the Steam-matched sample; the console-inclusive replication (N = 803) is reported alongside throughout.
  • Correlational. No causal claim; marketing budgets plausibly drive both ratings’ visibility and sales.
  • Coverage. The Metacritic scrape misses roughly a third of IGN’s output.

Rating → stimulus: the mean function

Per rating point, both stimulus measures — Steam reviews and peak concurrent players — multiply, but not by a constant factor. The step ratios accelerate going up the scale, which is what a stretched-exponential mean function predicts, and what a power law in the raw stimulus cannot produce: a power law predicts decelerating step ratios. Scripts: 05_analysis.R, 07_functional_form.R, 10_extended_outcomes.R, 16_upper_scale.R, 17_item_means_owners.R, 19_four_panel.R.

Per-step geometric means, both measures

Code 
fmt <- function(v) ifelse(is.na(v), "—", sprintf("%.2f", v))
steps <- read.csv(file.path(pd, "05_per_step_table.csv")) |>
  filter(ign_score_10 >= 5) |>
  mutate(ratio = geom_mean_reviews / lag(geom_mean_reviews),
         ror = ratio / lag(ratio))
ccu <- read.csv(file.path(pd, "10_per_step_extended.csv")) |>
  filter(ign_score_10 >= 5) |>
  mutate(ccu_ratio = geom_peak_ccu / lag(geom_peak_ccu),
         cror = ccu_ratio / lag(ccu_ratio))
left_join(steps, ccu, by = "ign_score_10") |>
  transmute(`IGN rating` = ign_score_10,
            `n` = n.y,
            `Geom. mean peak players` = round(geom_peak_ccu),
            `Ratio` = fmt(ccu_ratio),
            `Ratio ×` = fmt(cror),
            `n ` = n.x,
            `Geom. mean reviews` = round(geom_mean_reviews),
            `Ratio ` = fmt(ratio),
            `Ratio × ` = fmt(ror)) |>
  kable(align = "rrrrrrrrr")

Every step is worth more than the one below it on both measures, and the increments themselves grow: peak concurrent players go ×1.32, ×1.53, ×1.84, ×2.09, and finally ×3.33 for the 9 → 10 step; reviews corroborate with ×1.35, ×2.11, ×1.56, ×2.65, ×4.07 — the same acceleration, with the biggest jump at the top, on both a pure play-behavior measure and a sales proxy.

The Ratio × columns show the growth of the jumps themselves — each step’s ratio divided by the previous step’s. For peak players the chain is strikingly steady: 1.32 → (×1.16) → 1.53 → (×1.21) → 1.84 → (×1.13) → 2.09 → (×1.59) → 3.33. The reviews chain is noisier through the 7–8 dip (script 69’s bootstrap says that dip is sampling noise). One precision, so the table isn’t over-read: under the geometric model the exactly constant quantity is not ratio ÷ previous ratio but the ratio of their logarithms — the category widths — with ln(ratio) growing by the factor r each step, i.e. each ratio is the previous ratio raised to the power r. The raw Ratio × column is the easier-to-see shadow of that compounding, and it drifts upward slowly rather than sitting perfectly still.

To be precise about the sense in which ratios are “constant” here: the per-step stimulus ratio is not constant — a fixed stimulus ratio per step is exactly the logarithmic (Fechnerian) model that loses everywhere below. What is constant is one log up: each category’s width in log-stimulus units (the number of orders of magnitude of stimulus it spans) is r ≈ 1.24 times the width of the category below, so the raw per-step stimulus ratios compound geometrically (each step’s ratio is roughly the previous step’s ratio raised to the power r). Fixed log-stimulus ratios, not fixed stimulus ratios; the threshold plot in Section 5 shows this directly as a straight line of widths on a log axis.

The data, both stimulus measures

Figure 4 shows the full picture on both stimulus measures. To orient: each black point is one game (jittered vertically within its score row); the white points are the category geometric means; the dashed line is Fechner’s law — fixed stimulus ratios per step; the solid line is the stretched-exponential law’s observable form — fixed log-stimulus ratios per step. The stimulus axis is logarithmic, so the logarithmic model is a straight line in these coordinates and the stretched exponential bends away from it.

Functional-form race

NLS/OLS fits of log peak players on rating, ratings 5–10, n = 508 (from 73_form_comparison.csv; lower AIC = better, AIC = Akaike information criterion, a fit measure penalized for parameter count):

Code 
read.csv(file.path(pd, "73_form_comparison.csv")) |>
  mutate(AIC = round(AIC, 1), r2_raw = round(r2_raw, 3), r2_cat = round(r2_cat, 3)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Model", "Params", "AIC", "R² (games)", "R² (category means)"))

The stretched exponential is AIC-best, and on the category means the ordering is unambiguous: SE 0.999, quadratic 0.996, constant-ratio exponential 0.915, power law 0.843. The same race on the review-based samples replicates (SE best over the exponential by ΔAIC ≈ 4 Steam / ≈ 19 console-inclusive, over the power law by ≈ 11 / ≈ 29; 16_comparison.csv). The reason the power law dies is visible in the predicted step ratios (from 73_step_ratios.csv): observed ratios rise from 1.32 to 3.33, the exponential holds them constant at 1.78, and the power law makes them fall:

Code 
read.csv(file.path(pd, "73_step_ratios.csv")) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Step", "Observed", "Exponential", "Power law", "Quadratic", "SE"))

The SE β is identified only up to the log base of the score = log ψ reading (see 13_results.json note); the threshold-based estimate ln r ≈ 0.22 is the base-e value for the primary sample (β̂ = 0.32 from the NLS mean function).

Category means are almost exactly SE

Game-level noise is large (game-level R² ≈ 0.11 on players, ≈ 0.20 on reviews), but the category means are captured almost perfectly. On the primary measure the SE explains 99.9% of the category-mean variance vs 91.5% for the constant-ratio model (73_results.json); the review-based samples replicate (from 17_item_level.csv):

Code 
read.csv(file.path(pd, "17_item_level.csv")) |>
  filter(sample %in% c("steam_5to10", "full_5to10")) |>
  transmute(Sample = ifelse(sample == "steam_5to10", "Steam (N = 560)",
                            "Console-inclusive (N = 803)"),
            `k categories` = k_items,
            `R² linear` = round(r2_linear, 3), `R² SE` = round(r2_se, 3)) |>
  kable()

The SE curve explains 99.6% of the variance in category-mean log stimulus in both samples, vs 94.6% / 88.3% for the linear (constant-ratio) model.

Not a reviewing artifact

The primary measure settles the obvious confound by construction: peak concurrent players contains no review-writing anywhere in its pipeline, so “higher ratings just attract more reviewing” cannot produce its acceleration. For the secondary, review-count measure, two further checks say the same:

  • Decomposition (script 17, SteamSpy owner brackets): β_reviews 0.594 = β_owners 0.532 (90%) + β_rate 0.062 (10%); the acceleration (quadratic term) sits in owners (p = .008), not in reviews-per-owner (p = .83).
  • Elasticity (script 18): dev-reported sales scale as reviews^1.087 — the propensity-confound direction (b < 1) is contradicted.

Supplement: thresholds and the graded response model

The mean-function evidence above is the page’s spine; this section is the psychometric supplement that reads the same structure off the thresholds.

The model

Treat the rating as a graded item in the sense of item response theory: the graded response model (GRM — the standard psychometric model for ordered categories, and the workhorse of modern test scoring) places a set of ordered thresholds on an underlying continuum, and a response lands in category k when the underlying value falls between thresholds k−1 and k, up to Gaussian judgment noise. Anchoring the underlying continuum to log stimulus puts the thresholds in log-stimulus units, and the object of interest is the spacing between successive thresholds — the category widths. Scripts: 08_probit_thresholds.R, 11_range_frequency.R, 13_se_grm.R, 16_upper_scale.R, 22_theory_tests.R, 73_ccu_primary.R.

Threshold-spacing constraints compared, by AIC:

  • equidistant — equal widths in log stimulus (the Fechnerian reading; 3 params),
  • geometric — widths grow by a constant ratio r per step (4 params),
  • quantile / equal-mass — thresholds at the stimulus quantiles matching category frequencies,
  • free — every threshold estimated separately.

Anchor space: log beats raw

The categorization is linear in log stimulus, not raw stimulus: on the primary measure, anchoring the free-threshold model on log players beats raw players by ΔAIC = 42.8 (script 73); on reviews, log beats raw by ΔAIC = 78.5 (script 08).

Boundaries and widths

Code 
w <- read.csv(file.path(pd, "73_boundaries.csv"))
w |> transmute(`Boundary` = boundary,
               `Boundary (log players)` = round(logC, 2),
               `Boundary (raw players)` = format(round(players), big.mark = ","),
               `Width below boundary (log-player units)` = round(width_logC, 2)) |>
  kable()

Equidistant widths are rejected on the primary measure: likelihood-ratio χ² = 27.5, df = 3, p = 4.5 × 10⁻⁶ (script 73; the review-based tests agree — χ² = 33.5, p = 2.5 × 10⁻⁷ Steam and χ² = 36.2, p = 6.9 × 10⁻⁸ console-inclusive, script 16). Widths grow from 3.3 to 7.3 log-player units, and the top boundary extrapolates absurdly past the observed range: the 9|10 boundary sits at ≈ 1.2 billion simultaneous players — no observed stimulus level guarantees a 10.

Code 
wp <- w |> filter(is.finite(width_logC))
wp$idx <- seq_len(nrow(wp))
r_hat <- r73$geometric_r
ref <- tibble::tibble(idx = wp$idx,
  width = exp(mean(log(wp$width_logC)) + log(r_hat) * (wp$idx - mean(wp$idx))))
ggplot(wp, aes(idx, width_logC)) +
  geom_line(data = ref, aes(idx, width), linetype = "dashed", color = "gray60") +
  geom_point(shape = 21, fill = "white", stroke = 0.8, size = 3) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(3, 4, 5, 6, 8)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = wp$idx, labels = wp$boundary) +
  annotate("text", x = Inf, y = min(wp$width_logC), hjust = 1.1, vjust = 1.3,
           size = 3, label = paste0("r = ", round(r_hat, 3))) +
  labs(x = "Category boundary", y = "Width (log-player units)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 11) + theme(aspect.ratio = 1)

The threshold tournament

Code 
read.csv(file.path(pd, "73_threshold_models.csv")) |>
  mutate(AIC = round(AIC, 1)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Threshold family", "Params", "AIC"))

Geometric widths win outright: r = 1.244, beating even the fully flexible model on AIC despite the flexible model’s extra parameters, with equidistant spacing 22.4 AIC behind. The review-based samples replicate: geometric wins outright there too, r = 1.269 (Steam) and r = 1.234 (console-inclusive; script 16), and on the full nine-score data the tournament additionally rejects quantile/equal-mass spacing by ΔAIC > 1000 (script 11).

One bookkeeping note, so the page’s two headline constants don’t look contradictory: the mean-function β and the tournament’s r are the same dial measured with two instruments. If the category boundaries lie on the fitted curve, each width is e^β times the width below — r = e^β by algebra, not as an extra empirical claim. But the two are estimated differently: β̂ by fitting the smooth curve through the category means, r̂ by maximum likelihood on the full response distribution. With noisy data the instruments disagree a little — on the primary sample β̂ = 0.32 implies r ≈ 1.38, while the tournament gives r̂ = 1.24, implying β ≈ 0.22. A within-rating bootstrap (script 76, B = 1,000 per sample) shows the gap is statistically nothing: β̂ − ln r̂ = 0.13 with 95% CI [−0.11, 0.45] on the primary sample (reviews: 0.07, [−0.12, 0.30]), and the two estimates move together across resamples (cor = 0.84 and 0.90). The same bootstrap also says which instrument to trust: ln r̂ is pinned to about ±5% ([0.21, 0.23]), while β̂ — fit through just six category means — swings across [0.10, 0.68]. The two are one constant measured twice; the threshold-based r is the well-measured reading, and the tournament’s r is what this page treats as the estimate.

Range, not frequency

Two results against a frequency/rank reading (Parducci’s (1965) frequency principle; the rank/CDF anchor is the efficient-coding reading of Bhui & Gershman (2018); script 11):

  • The rank anchor loses to log magnitude, AIC 1837.7 vs 1827.3, and adds nothing on top of it (1828.0).
  • Category use is wildly non-uniform (observed shares vs uniform: χ² p ≈ 10⁻¹¹⁹) — raters do not equalize category frequencies.

The Parducci range weight pins at the boundary (w = 1.0), but range and frequency predictions correlate 0.98 here, so w is not separately identified; the anchor AIC comparison carries the conclusion.

GRM readings

A graded response model (GRM — the standard item-response-theory model for ordered categories) fit two ways (script 13): frequencies-only (latent trait θ ~ N(0,1); thresholds are normal quantiles of the cumulative category shares) and anchored (θ = standardized log stimulus — the model used throughout this section).

Code 
r13 <- read_json(file.path(pd, "13_results.json"))
tibble::tibble(
  Reading = c("Frequencies-only (θ ~ N(0,1))", "Anchored (θ = std log N)"),
  `Geometric ratio of threshold spacings` =
    c(r13$grm_freq_geo_ratio, r13$grm_anchored_geo_ratio)
) |> kable()

The two sets of thresholds correlate 1 — the geometric spacing is invariant to anchoring, because log stimulus is approximately normal over the reviewed set.

Head-to-head threshold-model likelihood race

Script 22 races full threshold theories (not just families) on IGN 5–10 and on the stellar data of Section 6:

Code 
read.csv(file.path(pd, "22_probit_race.csv")) |>
  mutate(AIC = round(AIC, 1), shape = round(shape, 3)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Dataset", "Model", "Params", "AIC", "Shape param"))

The exact-SE/geometric model wins against its 4-parameter rivals in both datasets. A free-offset log-power model converges to the exact-SE solution as its exponent α → 0 (the Box–Cox limit); the data sit at or near that small-α corner with an additive floor — the floor is essential (the zero-offset refit degenerates).

Stellar magnitudes

Data

Historical stellar brightness catalogs in the Hipparchus tradition: 14 observers from Ptolemy (137 AD) through al-Sufi (964), Tycho Brahe (1598), Hevelius (1690), Flamsteed (1725), to Piazzi (1814), each assigning stars to magnitude classes 1 (brightest) – 6 (faintest). All 14 predate photometry — no instrument ever measured the brightness; every magnitude is a human eye’s category judgment. The late catalogs (Flamsteed onward, including Lacaille 1751 and Piazzi 1814) were observed through telescopes — the eye still judged, but with optical gain and, by then, a heavily codified scale convention. Each historical class assignment is paired with the star’s modern flux from Hipparcos V-band photometry. Data are loaded read-only from the paper’s final repository, how_not_to_measure_repository (its script scripts/01_stars.R, evaluated up to data construction only; nothing in that repository is ever modified). Scripts here: 20_stellar_reanalysis.R, 69–71.

Mapping to the IGN battery: S = 7 − magnitude class (so higher S = brighter, like higher IGN = better), x = log relative flux (relative to the class-6 mean). Fractional/intermediate class assignments are excluded.

The analysis sample is the pre-telescope sky. The 14 observers split into seven pre-telescopic (Ptolemy 137, al-Sufi 964, Wilhelm IV 1586, Tycho 1598, de Houtman 1603, Kepler 1627, Hevelius 1690 — all data collected before or without the telescope) and seven telescopic-era (Halley 1679 onward, whose positions came through optics while brightness was still judged by eye). Hevelius is the deliberate case: he worked decades into the telescope era and used telescopes for lunar and solar work, but refused telescopic sights for star measurements, arguing plain sights were just as accurate — the famous dispute with Hooke, which Halley’s 1679 visit to Danzig was sent to settle (and largely settled in Hevelius’s favor). His catalog is naked-eye by conviction, not by date. Telescopic depth is a real contaminant: it lets an observer put stars in class 6 (“faintest”) that are strictly fainter than anything a naked-eye observer ever rated — 52% of Lacaille’s stars appear in no other catalog, and unique stars are always the faint ones (script 71’s census). The raw catalogs also show the observers knew this: Flamsteed’s file contains classes 7–8 and Piazzi’s runs to 11 (all filtered out upstream by the ≤ 6 gate), while Lacaille’s catalog stops at 6 and lumps his telescope-only stars into it. The sample used on this page therefore keeps every pre-telescopic row and admits telescopic-era rows only for stars present in at least one pre-telescopic catalog: N = 8,446 integer class assignments (3,452 telescopic-era rows on post-telescope-only stars dropped). Alternative cuts — none of which change the conclusion — are in Section 6.6.

Per-class flux ratios accelerate — just like IGN

Code 
pc <- read.csv(file.path(pd, "71_per_class_preera.csv"))
pc |> mutate(ror = flux_ratio_vs_prev / lag(flux_ratio_vs_prev)) |>
  transmute(`S (7 − class)` = S, n,
            `Mean log relative flux` = round(m, 2),
            `Ratio` = ifelse(is.na(flux_ratio_vs_prev), "—",
                             sprintf("%.2f", flux_ratio_vs_prev)),
            `Ratio ×` = ifelse(is.na(ror), "—", sprintf("%.2f", ror))) |>
  kable(align = "rrrrr")

The step ratios climb monotonically, ×1.54 → ×1.70 → ×2.29 → ×2.62 → ×4.06 at the top step — compare IGN’s top step of ×4.07. Written as a compounding chain (the Ratio × column): 1.54 → (×1.10) → 1.70 → (×1.35) → 2.29 → (×1.14) → 2.62 → (×1.55) → 4.06 — every multiplier itself multiplies, by a factor hovering around ~1.1–1.6 with no trend. Pogson’s 1856 standardization of the magnitude scale assumed a constant ratio (2.512× per class); the historical assignments the scale was built on do not have constant ratios. (Section 6.6 additionally splits the sample by era.)

This turns out to answer a question Stevens left open. Stevens and Galanter (1957, pp. 397–398) identified the stellar magnitude scale as the oldest category scale on record, noted that their own laboratory category scales for star-like points of light came out concave upward against decibels (categories narrowing toward the bright end), and asked whether the pre-photometric stellar catalogs were really linear in decibels or curved the same way — closing, after sampling Flamsteed and Herschel and finding the history hard going, with “Perhaps someone better qualified than we are should try to answer this question.” The answer, sixty-nine years on: not linear, and curved the opposite way from their laboratory spots. Against decibels the historical scale is concave downward — the per-class step grows from ≈ 1.9 dB at the faint end to ≈ 6.1 dB at the bright end, straddling Pogson’s uniform 4 dB — the same direction of acceleration as every other battery on this page.

Mean-function race

Same battery as the IGN data (AIC for linear/constant-ratio, SE, quadratic, plus the power law in raw stimulus):

Code 
mfu <- r71$preera$battery$mean_function
aicv <- unlist(mfu$aic)   # order: linear, se, quadratic, power_raw
tibble::tibble(
  Model = c("Fixed stimulus ratios (Fechner/Pogson)",
            "Fixed log-stimulus ratios (SE law)",
            "Quadratic", "Power law in raw stimulus"),
  AIC = round(aicv[c(1, 2, 3, 4)], 1)
) |> kable()

The SE wins (β = 0.297 — nearly identical to IGN’s 0.31), the quadratic is close behind, the linear model trails by ~1,000 AIC, and the raw-stimulus power law is not in the race (~3,400 AIC behind the SE). Class-mean R²: linear 0.899 vs SE 0.9997 — the same near-perfect category-mean fit as IGN.

Thresholds

Code 
thu <- r71$preera$battery$thresholds$pooled
tibble::tibble(
  Family = c("Flexible", "Geometric", "Equidistant"),
  AIC = round(c(thu$flex_aic, thu$geom$aic, thu$equi$aic), 1)
) |> kable()

Equidistant spacing is rejected (ΔAIC = 225 vs geometric). The geometric ratio is r = 1.173 — in the same band as IGN’s 1.24–1.27. The flexible family beats geometric by 35 AIC — with n ≈ 8k the data can afford 3 extra parameters; the geometric ratio remains the summary of how the widths grow.

Per-observer stability

SE β fit separately per observer (observers with ≥ 500 assignments and enough classes; from 20_per_observer.csv):

Code 
read.csv(file.path(pd, "20_per_observer.csv")) |>
  filter(is.finite(se_beta)) |>
  transmute(Observer = observer, n, `SE β` = round(se_beta, 2)) |>
  arrange(desc(`SE β`)) |>
  kable()

Ptolemy (137 AD) and al-Sufi (964) land within a few hundredths of each other and of the IGN Steam-sample β = 0.31 — the acceleration is not an artifact of one observer or era.

Pre- vs post-telescope

The sample keeps the stars comparable across eras, but the two observer groups may still sit at different levels or behave differently. Two checks (script 71): a threshold model with a single era effect — one location shift for the telescopic-era observers, thresholds shared — and the battery run separately per era on this sample.

Code 
r70 <- read_json(file.path(pd, "70_results.json"))
tu <- r71$preera$battery$thresholds
tibble::tibble(
  `Threshold family` = c("Equidistant", "Geometric", "Flexible"),
  `AIC, pooled` = round(c(tu$pooled$equi$aic, tu$pooled$geom$aic, tu$pooled$flex_aic), 1),
  `AIC, era shift` = round(c(tu$era$equi$aic, tu$era$geom$aic, tu$era$flex_aic), 1)
) |> kable()

Results, stated plainly:

  • The acceleration survives the era control. Equidistant spacing is rejected with the era shift in the model (ΔAIC = 187 vs geometric), and the geometric ratio barely moves: r = 1.173 pooled vs r = 1.155 with the shift (the fitted post-telescope offset is -0.63 in judgment-noise units).
  • The two eras, analyzed separately: the seven pre-telescopic observers alone give r = 1.179 (n = 5,517, ΔAIC vs equidistant = 168); the seven telescopic-era observers, restricted to pre-telescope-era stars, give r = 1.081 (n = 2,929, ΔAIC = 14) — the convention-era raters are much closer to log-linear, but even they never favor equidistant spacing.
  • Recode instead of exclude: assigning the telescopic-era observers’ post-telescope-only class-6 stars to a class 7 — historically defensible, since Galileo proposed a seventh magnitude and Flamsteed’s and Piazzi’s own catalogs contain classes 7–8 and 7–11 respectively (entries the ≤ 6 gate upstream removes), while Lacaille’s catalog lumps everything faint into 6 — keeps all 11,898 rows (3,158 recoded), and the K = 7 battery gives r = 1.303 with ΔAIC = 1,490 over equidistant: the seventh category extends the geometric ladder downward and the widths keep compounding.
  • Robustness across all sample choices: raw 14-catalog pool r = 1.235 (1.163 with per-observer fixed effects, script 70); unique-star class-6 exclusion only, r = 1.187 (1.144 FE); dropping Lacaille and Piazzi entirely, r = 1.206 (1.166 FE); strict four-observer naked-eye core, r = 1.185 (FE). Every variant rejects equidistant spacing.
  • Observers differ in how curved they are. Per-observer geometric r, fit on each observer’s full catalog (script 70; observers with ≥ 500 assignments; ΔAIC > 0 favors geometric over equidistant):
Code 
read.csv(file.path(pd, "70_per_observer_r.csv")) |>
  arrange(desc(r)) |>
  transmute(Observer = observer, n, r = round(r, 3),
            `ΔAIC (equidistant − geometric)` = round(d_aic, 1)) |>
  kable()

Tycho, Flamsteed, Hevelius, and al-Sufi are clearly geometric (ΔAIC +17 to +55); Ptolemy weakly so; the two most recent observers — Lacaille (1751) and Piazzi (1814), who judged brightness by eye through telescopes while conforming to a by-then heavily codified scale convention — are indistinguishable from log-linear on their full catalogs (r ≈ 1.03–1.06, ΔAIC ≈ 0). Their flatness stays in their own panels (script 70’s per-observer figure, figures/70_stellar_by_observer.png); per the robustness bullet above, no sample choice involving them changes the shared conclusion.

Word familiarity × word frequency

Data

Rating: word familiarity (FAM) from the Glasgow Norms (Scott et al. 2019) — 1–7 scale, item means over ~30 raters, rounded to integers here (an aggregate battery: the unit is the word, not the individual rater response). Stimulus (anchor): SUBTLEX-UK Zipf frequency (van Heuven et al. 2014) — Zipf = log₁₀ occurrences per billion words, already a log-scale quantity, from a British subtitle corpus matching the British raters. Words joined on lowercase spelling, parenthetical sense markers stripped; join n = 4,677 words. Scripts: 58_norms.R, 60_glasgow_cd.R (battery: 24_battery.R, validated by simulation in script 25 — the estimator recovers r = 1 on null data and r = 1.24 without bias across category counts and stimulus distributions).

Same battery, same pattern

Code 
g <- bind_rows(read.csv(file.path(pd, "58_norms.csv"))[1, ],
               read.csv(file.path(pd, "60_glasgow_cd.csv")))
g |> transmute(
  Battery = label, n, K,
  `Geometric r` = round(r_geom, 3),
  `ΔAIC equidistant − geometric` = round(d_aic_equi_minus_geom, 0),
  `SE β` = round(se_beta, 3),
  `R² category means (SE)` = round(r2_cat_se, 3),
  `R² category means (linear)` = round(r2_cat_lin, 3)
) |> kable()

Words rated one FAM step apart differ in corpus frequency by a growing multiplicative factor: geometric widths with r = 1.41, beating equidistant spacing by ~450 AIC. The SE mean function again captures the category means almost perfectly (R² = 0.998 vs 0.986 linear). The result is robust to the stimulus choice: contextual diversity (the number of distinct BBC programs a word appears in, an alternative SUBTLEX-UK exposure measure) gives r = 1.39.

Code

g60 <- read.csv(file.path(pd, "60_glasgow_cd.csv"))

tibble::tribble(
  ~Battery, ~Rating, ~Anchor, ~n, ~K, ~r,

  "Stellar magnitudes", "class 1–6, 14 observers 137–1814 AD", "log relative flux (Hipparcos V)",
    r71$preera$battery$n, 6, r71$preera$battery$thresholds$pooled$geom$r,
  "Word familiarity", "Glasgow FAM 1–7 (item means)", "SUBTLEX-UK Zipf",
    g58$n, 6, g58$r_geom,
  "Word familiarity (robustness)", "Glasgow FAM 1–7 (item means)", "SUBTLEX-UK contextual diversity",
    g60$n, 6, g60$r_geom
) |>
  mutate(r = round(r, 3)) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Battery", "Rating scale", "Stimulus (anchor)", "n", "K categories",
                      "Geometric r"))

In all six batteries the equidistant (Fechnerian) threshold model is rejected, the geometric-widths model wins or ties the flexible model on parsimony, the stretched-exponential mean function beats the linear one, and a raw-stimulus power law loses badly wherever it was raced.

Standing caveats

  • The IGN stimulus measures (review counts, user-rating counts, concurrent players) are outcome proxies for the judged magnitude, not unit sales and not quantities any reviewer observed; all IGN relations are correlational.
  • The word-familiarity batteries are aggregate-level (item means over raters), not individual responses.
  • The stellar sample is the pre-telescope sky: telescopic-era rows enter only for stars in ≥ 1 pre-telescopic catalog (3,452 rows dropped; Section 6). Across sample choices the headline ratio runs 1.081–1.303 (separate telescopic-era group at the bottom, class-7 recode at the top; page sample 1.173, era-controlled 1.155, raw pool 1.235) — equidistant is rejected in every variant. Per-observer r runs 1.03–1.27, all ≥ 1, with the two latest observers ≈ log-linear on their full catalogs.

## AI-assembled — not for publication
This page was assembled by an AI agent from the outputs of the registered analysis
scripts in `ign-ratings/scripts/` (see `scripts/REGISTRY.md`). Prose has not been
line-by-line verified by a human; do not publish or cite as-is. All statistics are
read directly from the scripts' `processed_data/` outputs, not recomputed here.
:::

## Overview

This page collects one set of analyses run identically across three very different
rating systems:

1. **IGN video game ratings** (integer 1–10, 2020–2025) against Steam outcome
   data — a purely **subjective, evaluative categorization**: game quality has
   no discernible objective correlate (no retinal neurons registering photons,
   not even an implicit tally of exposures — just an aesthetic/hedonic
   evaluation), yet that evaluation has real-world correlates we can measure,
   player counts and sales;
2. **historical stellar magnitudes** (brightness classes 1–6, assigned by 14
   observers from Ptolemy in 137 AD to Piazzi in 1814) against modern
   photometric flux — an **objective perceptual categorization**: a physical
   magnitude arriving at the eye, categorized by scientists *as a measurement*
   of that magnitude; and
3. **word familiarity norms** (Glasgow Norms, 1–7 scale) against corpus word
   frequency — an **experiential categorization of an objective quantity**:
   how often you encounter a word is an objective count, but nothing perceives
   it directly — the judgment reads accumulated experience out of memory.

The test is in that sense fully general: the same battery runs on a perceptual
categorization of a physical magnitude, a memory-based categorization of an
objective exposure count, and a pure aesthetic evaluation with no objective
correlate at all — three different kinds of judgment, three unrelated corners
of the space of things a rating scale can do. Finding the same spacing law in
all three would otherwise be what Meehl (1990), borrowing Wesley Salmon's
(1984) phrase, called a **damn strange coincidence**: theories earn credence by
predicting facts that, absent the theory, would be antecedently improbable —
and the agreement below is exactly that kind of fact.

One disambiguation, used strictly throughout: the IGN data come from video game
*reviews*, and the sales proxy is the count of Steam user *reviews* — two
different things that share a word. On this page, **rating** always refers to
the IGN 1–10 score, and **reviews** always refers to the Steam review count
(the sales proxy).

The same basic pattern appears in all three. Throughout, the objective quantity
paired with each rating — review counts, player counts, photometric flux, corpus
frequency — is called the **stimulus**: the magnitude the score is treated as
categorizing. When an ordinal rating scale is treated as a categorization of the
stimulus measured in **log-stimulus space**, the category boundaries are not
equally spaced. Instead each successive category is *wider* than the one below it
by a roughly constant multiplicative factor — a **geometric progression of
category widths**, with ratio r ≈ 1.24–1.27 for IGN ratings, r ≈ 1.17 for
stellar magnitudes (1.16 with a pre/post-telescope era control;
@sec-stellar-observers), and r ≈ 1.41 for word familiarity. Note what is and isn't constant:
the raw stimulus ratio per step is *not* constant (that would be a logarithmic
scale) — it is the step size *in log-stimulus coordinates* that grows by the
constant ratio r, so the raw per-step stimulus ratios themselves compound.

An equivalent description on the category means:

$$\log \Phi = c + A\,e^{\beta S},$$

where **Φ** is the stimulus (reviews, players, flux, corpus frequency), **S** is
the rating, **c** is an additive floor (the log-stimulus level the scale bottoms
out at), **A** is a scale constant, and **β** is the growth rate — the log of
the width ratio r, so β = ln r. In terms of the rating this says log-stimulus *compounds*:
each rating step multiplies (log Φ − c) by e^β = r. Under the reading
S = k·log ψ (ψ the latent magnitude) the same equation becomes
log Φ = c + A′·ψ^(βk) with βk < 1 — the **stretched exponential** in ψ from
which this page takes its name. One line to keep the fitted and the inferred
separate: what is *literally fit* to data, everywhere on this page, is the
S-space form — fixed log-stimulus ratios — and the analyses **test the SE law**
through that observable signature; the final step from the S-form to a
stretched exponential in ψ is inferred through S = k·log ψ, not fit. In every
dataset the fixed-log-stimulus-ratio mean function beats the fixed-stimulus-
ratio (Fechnerian) alternative, and a power law in the raw stimulus loses
badly. @sec-theory derives the form from first principles, introduces the
function properly, and says where it sits in the history of psychophysics.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-headline
#| tbl-cap: "Headline geometric ratios: the estimated common ratio r of successive category widths, per battery."
#| code-summary: "Read headline numbers from processed_data"
library(dplyr); library(jsonlite); library(knitr); library(ggplot2); library(tidyr)
pd <- "../processed_data"
r16 <- read_json(file.path(pd, "16_results.json"))
r73 <- read_json(file.path(pd, "73_results.json"))
r71 <- read_json(file.path(pd, "71_results.json"))
n58 <- read.csv(file.path(pd, "58_norms.csv"))[1, ]

tibble::tribble(
  ~Dataset, ~Rating, ~`Stimulus (log)`, ~n, ~`Geometric ratio r`,
  "IGN × peak concurrent players", "IGN 5–10 (integer era)", "log all-time peak concurrent players",
    r73$n, round(r73$geometric_r, 3),
  "IGN × Steam reviews", "IGN 5–10", "log Steam total reviews",
    r16$steam$n, round(r16$steam$geom_r, 3),
  "IGN console-inclusive", "IGN 5–10", "log Metacritic user-rating count",
    r16$full$n, round(r16$full$geom_r, 3),
  "Stellar magnitudes", "brightness class 1–6", "log relative flux (Hipparcos V)",
    r71$preera$battery$n, round(r71$preera$battery$thresholds$pooled$geom$r, 3),
  "Word familiarity", "Glasgow FAM 1–7 (rounded item means)", "SUBTLEX-UK Zipf frequency",
    n58$n, round(n58$r_geom, 3)
) |> kable()
```

Here **r** is the estimated common ratio of successive category widths, read
from the threshold spacing of a graded response model anchored to log stimulus
(the GRM — the standard psychometric model for ordered categories;
@sec-thresholds is the supplement that explains it); r = 1 would mean equally spaced categories in log stimulus
("Fechnerian" spacing — fixed *stimulus* ratios per category), r > 1 means
categories widen going up the scale (fixed *log-stimulus* ratios, per the title).

Gray dots = individual games / class assignments / words; open circles = category geometric means; solid = fixed log-stimulus ratios (the stretched-exponential law's observable form); dashed = fixed stimulus ratios (Fechner's law). **Reproducibility.** Every number on this page is read from `processed_data/`
